idiom_name: JCE SealedObject/Cipher behind a class + kotlinx.serialization custom serializer
implementation_notes: Kotlin runs on the JVM, so the protection mechanism is the JCE pair (Cipher plus SealedObject, or Cipher.doFinal over a serialized byte array) and the transfer object is an ordinary class whose protected map is a private property; kotlinx.serialization adds the language-level hook - a custom KSerializer, or @Transient plus a hand-written serializer, keeps the protected map out of the wire form and can seal it inside the encode path. What replaces the classic structure: the custom serializer replaces the TO's serialized data map and an overridden toString() replaces the masked-list rendering, while data-class generated methods have to be kept away from sensitive fields. The crypto itself is platform-supplied, which is why this realization is a library use rather than hand-written structure.
pitfalls: A data class synthesizes toString/equals/hashCode/copy over every constructor property: never put protected values in the primary constructor or the generated methods will print, copy and hash them.

@Transient requires a default value and is a serialization declaration, not a security control - the property still exists in memory and in reflection; clear the mutable collections after sealing and keep plaintext lifetimes short.

JVM interop is a hole: internal/private visibility is a compile-time promise, and Java code in the same module (or reflection) can still read the backing field, so only the sealed payload belongs in an accessible place.
SealedObject deserialization runs ObjectInputStream inside getObject - keep the sealed payload to JDK types and configure an ObjectInputFilter exactly as in Java.
